en.title: What Is the Communion of Saints?
en.question: The Apostles' Creed says "I believe in the communion of saints." What exactly does that mean, and how does it include people who have already died?

answer.summary:
> "The souls of the just are in the hand of God, and no torment shall touch them." — Wisdom 3:1

The Communion of Saints — *communio sanctorum* — is one of the most profound and consoling teachings of the Catholic faith, expressing the reality that death does not sever the bond between baptized members of Christ's Body. The phrase in the Apostles' Creed carries a dual meaning in the Latin original: *sanctorum* can refer to "holy persons" (saints) or to "holy things" (the sacred mysteries, especially the Eucharist). Together these meanings point to the same reality: the Church is one Body in Christ, sharing both in holy persons and in holy gifts, and this sharing transcends the boundary of physical death.

The Church exists in three states: the Church Militant (believers on earth), the Church Suffering (souls being purified in purgatory), and the Church Triumphant (saints in heaven). All three are united in one Body under Christ. Physical death changes a person's mode of existence but does not remove them from the Body. Paul's teaching that "whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's" (Romans 14:8) and his affirmation that "neither death nor life... shall be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 8:38–39) are the scriptural anchor. The unity of Christ's Body is stronger than the boundary between the living and the dead.

The scriptural evidence for ongoing communion across death is significant. Hebrews 12:1 speaks of "a great cloud of witnesses" surrounding the earthly Church — not merely past exemplars but present witnesses aware of the ongoing struggle. Hebrews 12:22–23 describes the earthly worship as being conducted "with the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven" and "the spirits of just men made perfect" — a liturgy simultaneously earthly and heavenly. Revelation 5:8 shows the elders in heaven presenting to God the prayers of the saints on earth, exercising an intercessory role even after death. These texts are not metaphors; they describe the theological reality the Church has always understood.

The key distinction is between **adoration** (latria) — belonging to God alone — and **communion** (fellowship, mutual support) — which the whole Body of Christ shares across the states of the Church. When Catholics ask saints to pray for them, they are not worshipping the saints; they are exercising the same mutual intercession that Paul urged living Christians to practice toward each other (Romans 15:30, Ephesians 6:18). The difference is that the saints in heaven pray with perfect charity, unimpeded by the distractions and weaknesses of earthly life.

The Catechism (CCC 946–962) devotes an extended treatment to the Communion of Saints, grounding it in the Eucharist ("the source and summit") as the great sacrament of unity. CCC 954 specifies: "The three states of the Church... form one Church." CCC 955 adds: "It is a single communion." The practical consequence is that the Church's life is always communal, never merely individual — Catholics pray not only as isolated individuals before God but as members of a living Body that includes the angels, the saints in glory, and the souls in purgatory, all united in Christ's one Body.

objections.response: Scripture depicts the dead in Christ as spiritually alive and aware, not cut off: "since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses" (Hebrews 12:1) pictures departed believers watching our race. The souls of the martyrs in heaven cry out about events on earth (Revelation 6:9-10), and Jesus describes the dead as conscious and able to see and care about the living (Luke 16:22-31). "Whether we live or die, we are the Lord's" (Romans 14:8) — death doesn't sever a believer's union with Christ or with the rest of his Body.
objections.objection: Once someone dies, their relationship to us on earth ends — the dead can't know what's happening among the living, so there is no ongoing "communion" with them.

objections.response: What Deuteronomy 18 forbids is occult divination — attempting to manipulate or extract hidden knowledge from spirits through forbidden magical rites. Asking the Church Triumphant in heaven to pray for us, the way we ask a friend on earth to pray for us, is not sorcery; it presupposes the same living communion within the Body of Christ that Paul describes when he asks living believers to pray for one another (1 Thessalonians 5:25; James 5:16).
objections.objection: Necromancy — consulting the dead — is explicitly condemned in Scripture: "There shall not be found among you... one who consults ghosts and spirits, or seeks oracles from the dead" (Deuteronomy 18:10-11). Praying for or with the dead falls under this same condemnation.

objections.response: Christ's mediation is unique and unrepeatable as the source of redemption (1 Timothy 2:5-6), but Scripture is full of subordinate intercession that flows entirely from Christ's mediation rather than competing with it — Paul asks believers to intercede for him (Romans 15:30), James commands, "pray for one another, that you may be healed" (James 5:16), and the communion of saints simply extends that same mutual intercession across the boundary of death, since all the baptized — living and dead — remain one Body in Christ (1 Corinthians 12:12-27).
objections.objection: Christ is our only mediator (1 Timothy 2:5), so praying with or for the saints in heaven, or asking them to pray for us, adds an unnecessary and unbiblical layer between believers and God.
